An unknown enzyme 'E' completely digests a biological polymer into its constituent monomers. The covalent bonds being broken by this enzyme were originally formed by a dehydration reaction between the carboxyl ($-COOH$) group of one monomer and the amino ($-NH_2$) group of the adjacent monomer.

Identify the class of enzyme 'E' and the specific name of the bond it hydrolyses.
questions.question:
An unknown enzyme 'E' completely digests a biological polymer into its constituent monomers. The covalent bonds being broken by this enzyme were originally formed by a dehydration reaction between the carboxyl ($-COOH$) group of one monomer and the amino ($-NH_2$) group of the adjacent monomer.

Identify the class of enzyme 'E' and the specific name of the bond it hydrolyses.
options: Amylase and Glycosidic bond
Lipase and Ester bond
Protease and Peptide bond
Nuclease and Phosphodiester bond
questions.solution:
The bond formed by a dehydration reaction (removal of a water molecule) between the carboxyl ($-COOH$) group of one monomer and the amino ($-NH_2$) group of the adjacent monomer is a peptide bond, which links amino acids.

Proteins are polymers of amino acids linked by these peptide bonds. The class of enzymes that hydrolyse peptide bonds to digest proteins into amino acids is protease.

Amylases break glycosidic bonds in carbohydrates, lipases break ester bonds in lipids, and nucleases break phosphodiester bonds in nucleic acids.

Answer: Protease and Peptide bond

Answer: Protease and Peptide bond

Read the following statements regarding the features of cloning vectors:
(A) The 'ori' sequence is responsible for controlling the copy number of the linked DNA.
(B) A cloning vector must have multiple recognition sites for a single restriction enzyme to ensure successful integration of alien DNA.
(C) Selectable markers help in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of the transformants.
(D) Normal E. coli cells do not carry resistance against antibiotics such as ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.question:
Read the following statements regarding the features of cloning vectors:
(A) The 'ori' sequence is responsible for controlling the copy number of the linked DNA.
(B) A cloning vector must have multiple recognition sites for a single restriction enzyme to ensure successful integration of alien DNA.
(C) Selectable markers help in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of the transformants.
(D) Normal E. coli cells do not carry resistance against antibiotics such as ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin.

How many of the above statements are correct?
options: One
Two
Four
Three
questions.solution:
Statement (A) is correct because the origin of replication (ori) is the sequence where replication starts, and it also controls the copy number of the linked DNA.

Statement (B) is incorrect because a cloning vector needs to have very few, preferably single, recognition sites for commonly used restriction enzymes. The presence of more than one recognition site within the vector will generate several fragments, which complicates the gene cloning process.

Statement (C) is correct as selectable markers are essential to identify and eliminate non-transformants while permitting the growth of transformants.

Statement (D) is correct because normal E. coli cells do not naturally carry resistance genes against antibiotics like ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, or kanamycin; these genes are introduced via vectors.

Therefore, three statements are correct.

Answer: Three

questions.q: A student prepares a reaction mixture for Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) by mixing the template DNA, primers, deoxynucleotides, and a normal DNA polymerase isolated from human cells in a single tube. The tube is then subjected to the standard temperature cycles of PCR. What will be the expected outcome of this reaction?
questions.question: A student prepares a reaction mixture for Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) by mixing the template DNA, primers, deoxynucleotides, and a normal DNA polymerase isolated from human cells in a single tube. The tube is then subjected to the standard temperature cycles of PCR. What will be the expected outcome of this reaction?
options: The gene will be amplified normally, but the process will take a longer time.
The primers will fail to bind to the complementary regions of the template DNA.
Exactly one complete copy of the target DNA will be synthesised before the reaction stops.
No amplification will occur because the enzyme will get denatured during the first heating step.
questions.solution:
In a standard Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), all components are mixed before the temperature cycles begin. The very first step of a PCR cycle is denaturation, which requires heating the reaction mixture to a high temperature to separate the double-stranded DNA.

Normal DNA polymerase isolated from human cells is not thermostable and will be permanently denatured (destroyed) by this high heat.

Because the enzyme is destroyed in the first step, it will not be able to extend the primers in the subsequent steps. As a result, no amplification of the DNA will occur.

This is why PCR requires a thermostable enzyme like Taq polymerase, which remains active even after high-temperature denaturation steps.

Answer: No amplification will occur because the enzyme will get denatured during the first heating step.

questions.q: A scientist attempts to create a transgenic dicot plant using an Agrobacterium-based vector. Upon observation, the plant successfully expresses the introduced gene of interest, but it also develops large crown gall tumors at the sites of infection. Which of the following is the most likely procedural error made by the scientist during the preparation of the vector?
questions.question: A scientist attempts to create a transgenic dicot plant using an Agrobacterium-based vector. Upon observation, the plant successfully expresses the introduced gene of interest, but it also develops large crown gall tumors at the sites of infection. Which of the following is the most likely procedural error made by the scientist during the preparation of the vector?
options: The gene of interest was inserted into the ori region of the plasmid.
The scientist used a retroviral vector instead of Agrobacterium.
The plant cells rejected the recombinant DNA after transformation.
The scientist failed to disarm the Ti plasmid before inserting the gene of interest.
questions.solution:
The development of crown gall tumors indicates that the wild-type T-DNA, which carries tumor-inducing genes, was successfully transferred to the plant cells.

For Agrobacterium tumefaciens to be used as a safe cloning vector, its Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmid must be 'disarmed' by removing the tumor-causing genes while retaining the DNA transfer mechanism.

Since the plant expresses the gene of interest, the transformation was successful, meaning the ori was intact (ruling out option 1) and the DNA was not rejected (ruling out option 3). Retroviruses are used to transform animal cells, not plants (ruling out option 2). The presence of tumors alongside the desired trait means the plasmid was not properly disarmed before use.

Answer: The scientist failed to disarm the Ti plasmid before inserting the gene of interest.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: A researcher sets up a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) starting with 4 copies of a specific target gene. At the end of the amplification process, the tube contains 1024 copies of the gene. Assuming 100% efficiency in every cycle, how many cycles of PCR were completed?
questions.question: A researcher sets up a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) starting with 4 copies of a specific target gene. At the end of the amplification process, the tube contains 1024 copies of the gene. Assuming 100% efficiency in every cycle, how many cycles of PCR were completed?
questions.solution:
The amplification of DNA during PCR follows an exponential growth pattern described by the equation:
Final number of copies = Initial number of copies $\times$ $2^n$
where $n$ is the number of cycles.

Given:
Initial copies = 4
Final copies = 1024

Substituting the values:
$1024 = 4 \times 2^n$
$2^n = \dfrac{1024}{4}$
$2^n = 256$

Since $2^8 = 256$, the number of cycles $n = 8$.

Choosing 10 is a mistake resulting from ignoring the initial 4 copies and assuming $2^{10} = 1024$. Choosing 16 is a mistake from incorrectly taking the square root of 256 instead of finding the base-2 exponent.

Answer: 8

questions.q: A foreign DNA fragment is ligated at the Pst I restriction site of the cloning vector pBR322. The resulting recombinant plasmids are transformed into E. coli cells. If these specific recombinant transformants are plated first on a tetracycline-containing medium and then replica-plated onto an ampicillin-containing medium, what will be their growth pattern?
questions.question: A foreign DNA fragment is ligated at the Pst I restriction site of the cloning vector pBR322. The resulting recombinant plasmids are transformed into E. coli cells. If these specific recombinant transformants are plated first on a tetracycline-containing medium and then replica-plated onto an ampicillin-containing medium, what will be their growth pattern?
options: They will grow on the tetracycline medium and will also grow when replica-plated onto the ampicillin medium.
They will grow on the tetracycline medium but will fail to grow when replica-plated onto the ampicillin medium.
They will fail to grow on the tetracycline medium but would grow if plated directly on the ampicillin medium.
They will fail to grow on both the tetracycline medium and the ampicillin medium.
questions.solution:
The cloning vector pBR322 has two antibiotic resistance genes: $amp^{R}$ (ampicillin resistance) and $tet^{R}$ (tetracycline resistance).

The restriction site for the enzyme Pst I is located within the $amp^{R}$ gene. When a foreign DNA is inserted at the Pst I site, the $amp^{R}$ gene is disrupted due to insertional inactivation. As a result, the recombinant plasmid loses its ability to confer resistance to ampicillin, but the $tet^{R}$ gene remains intact.

Therefore, these recombinant transformants are resistant to tetracycline but sensitive to ampicillin. When plated first on a tetracycline-containing medium, they will successfully grow and form colonies. However, when these colonies are replica-plated onto an ampicillin-containing medium, they will fail to grow due to the loss of ampicillin resistance.

Answer: They will grow on the tetracycline medium but will fail to grow when replica-plated onto the ampicillin medium.

questions.q: A student attempts to perform a Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) using normal DNA polymerase isolated from Escherichia coli instead of the standard Taq polymerase. If the standard three-step temperature cycle is applied, what mandatory modification must be made to the protocol for successful DNA amplification to occur over multiple cycles?
questions.question: A student attempts to perform a Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) using normal DNA polymerase isolated from Escherichia coli instead of the standard Taq polymerase. If the standard three-step temperature cycle is applied, what mandatory modification must be made to the protocol for successful DNA amplification to occur over multiple cycles?
options: The denaturation temperature must be lowered to $37^{\circ}\text{C}$ to prevent the enzyme from degrading.
Fresh DNA polymerase must be added manually before the extension step of every single cycle.
The enzyme must be added only once, immediately after the first denaturation step is completed.
Fresh primers must be added after every cycle to compensate for the lack of thermostability.
questions.solution:
The standard PCR protocol involves a denaturation step at a very high temperature (approximately $94^{\circ}\text{C}$). Normal DNA polymerase isolated from Escherichia coli is not thermostable and will denature and lose its catalytic activity at this high temperature.

If Escherichia coli DNA polymerase is used, it will be destroyed during the denaturation step of each cycle. Therefore, to achieve amplification over multiple cycles, fresh enzyme must be added manually after denaturation and annealing, right before the extension step of every single cycle.

Lowering the denaturation temperature to $37^{\circ}\text{C}$ would fail to separate the double-stranded DNA. Adding the enzyme only once after the first denaturation would only allow one cycle of amplification, as the enzyme would be destroyed in the second cycle's denaturation step. Primers are not enzymes and their consumption is not related to the thermostability of the polymerase.

Answer: Fresh DNA polymerase must be added manually before the extension step of every single cycle.
questions.explanation:
The standard PCR protocol involves a denaturation step at a very high temperature (approximately $94^{\circ}\text{C}$). Normal DNA polymerase isolated from Escherichia coli is not thermostable and will denature and lose its catalytic activity at this high temperature.

If Escherichia coli DNA polymerase is used, it will be destroyed during the denaturation step of each cycle. Therefore, to achieve amplification over multiple cycles, fresh enzyme must be added manually after denaturation and annealing, right before the extension step of every single cycle.

Lowering the denaturation temperature to $37^{\circ}\text{C}$ would fail to separate the double-stranded DNA. Adding the enzyme only once after the first denaturation would only allow one cycle of amplification, as the enzyme would be destroyed in the second cycle's denaturation step. Primers are not enzymes and their consumption is not related to the thermostability of the polymerase.

Answer: Fresh DNA polymerase must be added manually before the extension step of every single cycle.

options: Exponential phase
Stationary phase
Lag phase
Decline phase
questions.solution:
In a continuous culture system, the used medium is continuously drained out from one side while fresh medium is added from the other.

This constant replenishment of nutrients and removal of waste products prevents the depletion of resources and the accumulation of toxins.

As a result, the cells are maintained in their physiologically most active state, which is the log or exponential phase of the microbial growth curve, thereby achieving maximum productivity.

The lag phase is the initial adaptation period, the stationary phase occurs when nutrients are depleted, and the decline phase is when cell death exceeds division.

Answer: Exponential phase

Assertion (A): Agrobacterium tumefaciens is widely used as a cloning vector for delivering desirable genes into plant cells.
Reason (R): The Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium is disarmed to eliminate its pathogenicity while retaining its ability to transfer DNA into the host plant.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true

questions.solution:

The disease-causing genes are removed (disarmed) so it is no longer pathogenic, but it retains the mechanism to deliver desirable genes into the plant genome.

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

Assertion (A): The stickiness of DNA ends produced by certain restriction enzymes facilitates the action of the enzyme DNA ligase.
Reason (R): Restriction endonucleases cut the strand of DNA a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The stickiness of DNA ends produced by certain restriction enzymes facilitates the action of the enzyme DNA ligase.
Reason (R): Restriction endonucleases cut the strand of DNA a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true because the sticky ends form temporary hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts. This brings the DNA fragments close together, which facilitates the joining action of DNA ligase to form phosphodiester bonds.

Reason (R) is also true because restriction enzymes that produce sticky ends do so by cutting the DNA strand a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites, but between the same two bases on the opposite strands.

However, Reason (R) explains how sticky ends are formed, not why their stickiness facilitates the action of DNA ligase. The correct explanation for Assertion (A) is the formation of hydrogen bonds between the complementary overhangs. Therefore, both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

questions.q: Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a pathogen of several dicot plants, is able to deliver a piece of DNA known as 'T-DNA' to transform normal plant cells into a tumor. What specific modification is made to its naturally occurring Ti plasmid so that it can be used as a cloning vector for plants?
questions.question: Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a pathogen of several dicot plants, is able to deliver a piece of DNA known as 'T-DNA' to transform normal plant cells into a tumor. What specific modification is made to its naturally occurring Ti plasmid so that it can be used as a cloning vector for plants?
options: The entire T-DNA region is deleted to prevent the formation of tumors in the host plant.
An animal origin of replication is added to allow its multiplication in a wider range of hosts.
Ampicillin resistance genes are introduced to facilitate the infection of plant cells.
The tumor-causing genes are removed, but the plasmid retains its mechanism to deliver the DNA of interest.
questions.solution:
The tumor inducing (Ti) plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens has been modified into a cloning vector which is no more pathogenic to the plants but is still able to use the mechanisms to deliver genes of our interest into a variety of plants.

This is achieved by 'disarming' the plasmid, which involves removing the pathogenic (tumor-causing) genes from the T-DNA region while retaining the sequences necessary for the transfer of DNA into the plant cell.

Deleting the entire T-DNA region would destroy its ability to transfer DNA. Adding an animal origin of replication or ampicillin resistance does not relate to its primary modification for use as a plant vector.

Answer: The tumor-causing genes are removed, but the plasmid retains its mechanism to deliver the DNA of interest.
questions.explanation:
The tumor inducing (Ti) plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens has been modified into a cloning vector which is no more pathogenic to the plants but is still able to use the mechanisms to deliver genes of our interest into a variety of plants.

This is achieved by 'disarming' the plasmid, which involves removing the pathogenic (tumor-causing) genes from the T-DNA region while retaining the sequences necessary for the transfer of DNA into the plant cell.

Deleting the entire T-DNA region would destroy its ability to transfer DNA. Adding an animal origin of replication or ampicillin resistance does not relate to its primary modification for use as a plant vector.

Answer: The tumor-causing genes are removed, but the plasmid retains its mechanism to deliver the DNA of interest.

questions.q: Which of the following representations correctly shows the palindromic sequence and the exact cleavage sites (indicated by arrows) for the restriction endonuclease EcoRI?
questions.question: Which of the following representations correctly shows the palindromic sequence and the exact cleavage sites (indicated by arrows) for the restriction endonuclease EcoRI?
options:
5' G A A $\downarrow$ T T C 3'
3' C T T $\uparrow$ A A G 5'

5' G A A T T $\downarrow$ C 3'
3' C $\uparrow$ T T A A G 5'

5' G $\downarrow$ A A T T C 3'
3' C $\uparrow$ T T A A G 5'

5' G $\downarrow$ A A T T C 3'
3' C T T A A $\uparrow$ G 5'
questions.solution:
EcoRI recognizes the 6-base pair palindromic sequence 5' - G A A T T C - 3'.

It does not cut exactly in the center of the palindrome (which would produce blunt ends). Instead, it cuts between the same two bases on the opposite strands, specifically between the G and A bases.

This staggered cut generates overhanging stretches called sticky ends.

Therefore, the correct cleavage site is between G and A on the 5' $\rightarrow$ 3' strand, and between A and G on the 3' $\rightarrow$ 5' strand.

Answer: 5' G $\downarrow$ A A T T C 3'
3' C T T A A $\uparrow$ G 5'
questions.explanation:
EcoRI recognizes the 6-base pair palindromic sequence 5' - G A A T T C - 3'.

It does not cut exactly in the center of the palindrome (which would produce blunt ends). Instead, it cuts between the same two bases on the opposite strands, specifically between the G and A bases.

This staggered cut generates overhanging stretches called sticky ends.

Therefore, the correct cleavage site is between G and A on the 5' $\rightarrow$ 3' strand, and between A and G on the 3' $\rightarrow$ 5' strand.

Answer: 5' G $\downarrow$ A A T T C 3'
3' C T T A A $\uparrow$ G 5'

questions.q: During agarose gel electrophoresis, a mixture of DNA fragments is loaded into the wells. Which of the following correctly describes the nature of DNA molecules and their direction of movement under an electric field?
questions.question: During agarose gel electrophoresis, a mixture of DNA fragments is loaded into the wells. Which of the following correctly describes the nature of DNA molecules and their direction of movement under an electric field?
options: Positively charged; move towards the cathode
Negatively charged; move towards the anode
Negatively charged; move towards the cathode
Positively charged; move towards the anode
questions.solution:
DNA molecules possess a sugar-phosphate backbone, which imparts a net negative charge to them. During gel electrophoresis, when an electric field is applied, these negatively charged DNA fragments are forced to migrate towards the positive electrode, which is the anode.

Options 1 and 4 are incorrect because DNA is not positively charged. Option 3 is incorrect because negatively charged molecules move towards the anode, not the cathode.

Answer: Negatively charged; move towards the anode
questions.explanation:

questions.question:
Read the following statements regarding the tools used in recombinant DNA technology:

I. Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of DNA.
II. Endonucleases make cuts at specific positions within the DNA.
III. DNA ligase facilitates the joining of DNA fragments by forming hydrogen bonds between them.
IV. Taq polymerase is isolated from a thermophilic bacterium and extends primers during PCR.

How many of the given statements are correct?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
questions.solution:
Statement I is correct as exonucleases remove nucleotides from the free ends of DNA.

Statement II is correct as endonucleases make cuts at specific positions within the DNA duplex.

Statement III is incorrect because DNA ligase joins DNA fragments by forming covalent phosphodiester bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone, not hydrogen bonds (hydrogen bonds form spontaneously between complementary sticky ends).

Statement IV is correct as Taq polymerase is a thermostable enzyme isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus and is used to extend primers on a genomic DNA template during PCR.

Therefore, exactly three statements are correct.

Answer: Three
questions.explanation:
Statement I is correct as exonucleases remove nucleotides from the free ends of DNA.

Statement II is correct as endonucleases make cuts at specific positions within the DNA duplex.

Statement III is incorrect because DNA ligase joins DNA fragments by forming covalent phosphodiester bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone, not hydrogen bonds (hydrogen bonds form spontaneously between complementary sticky ends).

Statement IV is correct as Taq polymerase is a thermostable enzyme isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus and is used to extend primers on a genomic DNA template during PCR.

Therefore, exactly three statements are correct.

Answer: Three

questions.question:
Read the following statements regarding the selection of recombinants using a chromogenic substrate:
A. The enzyme $\beta$-galactosidase acts on a chromogenic substrate to produce a blue colour.
B. Insertion of foreign DNA into the coding sequence of $\beta$-galactosidase results in its insertional inactivation.
C. Bacterial colonies having plasmids with the foreign insert produce blue coloured colonies.
D. Non-recombinant colonies fail to produce any colour due to the absence of the enzyme.

How many of the above statements are correct?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
questions.solution:
Statement A is correct. The intact $\beta$-galactosidase enzyme acts on a chromogenic substrate to produce a blue-coloured product.

Statement B is correct. When foreign DNA is inserted into the coding sequence of the $\beta$-galactosidase gene, the gene is insertionally inactivated and loses its function.

Statement C is incorrect. Bacterial colonies with the foreign insert (recombinants) have an inactivated enzyme and therefore do not produce any colour (they appear white).

Statement D is incorrect. Non-recombinant colonies have an intact $\beta$-galactosidase gene, produce the functional enzyme, and thus give blue coloured colonies.

Therefore, exactly two statements (A and B) are correct.

Answer: Two

Statement D is incorrect. Non-recombinant colonies have an intact $\beta$-galactosidase gene, produce the functional enzyme, and thus give blue coloured colonies.

Therefore, exactly two statements (A and B) are correct.

Answer: Two

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
questions.question:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The process of elution is essential for isolating purified DNA fragments from an agarose gel for recombinant DNA construction.

Reason (R): DNA fragments separated on the gel can only be visualised after staining with ethidium bromide and exposure to UV radiation.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true because the separated bands of DNA are cut out from the agarose gel and extracted from the gel piece. This step, known as elution, is necessary to obtain purified DNA fragments for constructing recombinant DNA by joining them with cloning vectors.

Reason (R) is also true because DNA fragments cannot be seen in visible light; they must be stained with ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation to be visualised as bright orange bands.

However, Reason (R) is not the correct explanation for Assertion (A). Visualization is a prerequisite to locate the DNA bands, but the fundamental reason for performing elution is to physically extract the DNA for downstream processes like ligation, not merely because it requires staining.

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

Reason (R) is also true because DNA fragments cannot be seen in visible light; they must be stained with ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation to be visualised as bright orange bands.

However, Reason (R) is not the correct explanation for Assertion (A). Visualization is a prerequisite to locate the DNA bands, but the fundamental reason for performing elution is to physically extract the DNA for downstream processes like ligation, not merely because it requires staining.

questions.q: When a restriction endonuclease cuts both the vector and the foreign DNA a little away from the centre of their respective palindromic sites, it generates single-stranded overhanging stretches at the ends. What specific advantage does this cutting pattern provide during the construction of a recombinant DNA molecule?
questions.question: When a restriction endonuclease cuts both the vector and the foreign DNA a little away from the centre of their respective palindromic sites, it generates single-stranded overhanging stretches at the ends. What specific advantage does this cutting pattern provide during the construction of a recombinant DNA molecule?
options: It prevents the action of exonucleases from degrading the newly exposed DNA ends.
It provides a free 3'-OH group that allows DNA polymerase to easily synthesize a new complementary strand.
It ensures that the recombinant DNA molecule can easily undergo transformation into the competent host cell.
It produces sticky ends that form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts, facilitating the action of DNA ligase.
questions.solution:
Restriction endonucleases that cut the DNA strand a little away from the centre of the palindromic sites generate single-stranded overhanging stretches called sticky ends.

These ends are called sticky because they readily form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts. This stickiness of the ends specifically facilitates the action of the enzyme DNA ligase, which joins the foreign DNA and vector DNA molecules together to form a stable recombinant DNA.

The sticky ends do not prevent exonuclease action, nor are they primarily generated to allow DNA polymerase extension or to directly facilitate transformation into the host cell.

Answer: It produces sticky ends that form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts, facilitating the action of DNA ligase.
questions.explanation:
Restriction endonucleases that cut the DNA strand a little away from the centre of the palindromic sites generate single-stranded overhanging stretches called sticky ends.

These ends are called sticky because they readily form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts. This stickiness of the ends specifically facilitates the action of the enzyme DNA ligase, which joins the foreign DNA and vector DNA molecules together to form a stable recombinant DNA.

The sticky ends do not prevent exonuclease action, nor are they primarily generated to allow DNA polymerase extension or to directly facilitate transformation into the host cell.

Answer: It produces sticky ends that form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts, facilitating the action of DNA ligase.

When these cells are plated on different media, the recombinant colonies are found to survive on a medium containing tetracycline but fail to grow on a medium containing ampicillin. Which of the following restriction endonucleases was most likely used to insert the foreign DNA into the vector?
questions.question: A researcher has generated recombinant E. coli cells using the pBR322 cloning vector. When these cells are plated on different media, the recombinant colonies are found to survive on a medium containing tetracycline but fail to grow on a medium containing ampicillin. Which of the following restriction endonucleases was most likely used to insert the foreign DNA into the vector?
options: Bam HI
Sal I
Eco RI
Pst I
questions.solution:
The recombinant cells survive on tetracycline, which means the tetracycline resistance gene ($tet^R$) is intact and functional. However, they fail to grow on ampicillin, indicating that the ampicillin resistance gene ($amp^R$) has lost its function due to insertional inactivation.

Therefore, the foreign DNA must have been inserted at a restriction site located within the $amp^R$ gene. In the pBR322 vector, the restriction sites for Pst I and Pvu I are located within the $amp^R$ gene. Bam HI and Sal I sites are located within the $tet^R$ gene, while the Eco RI site is located outside both selectable markers.

Answer: Pst I
questions.explanation:

Therefore, the foreign DNA must have been inserted at a restriction site located within the $amp^R$ gene. In the pBR322 vector, the restriction sites for Pst I and Pvu I are located within the $amp^R$ gene. Bam HI and Sal I sites are located within the $tet^R$ gene, while the Eco RI site is located outside both selectable markers.

Answer: Pst I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.q: In recombinant DNA technology, various methods are employed to introduce alien DNA into host cells. Which of the following is a direct (vectorless) method of gene transfer?
questions.question: In recombinant DNA technology, various methods are employed to introduce alien DNA into host cells. Which of the following is a direct (vectorless) method of gene transfer?
options: Agrobacterium-mediated transfer
Retrovirus infection
Bacteriophage infection
Micro-injection
questions.solution:
Agrobacterium tumefaciens, retroviruses, and bacteriophages act as biological vectors to carry and deliver foreign DNA into specific host cells.

Micro-injection is a direct (vectorless) method of gene transfer in which recombinant DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell using a micro-pipette, without the involvement of any biological vector.

Answer: Micro-injection
questions.explanation:
Agrobacterium tumefaciens, retroviruses, and bacteriophages act as biological vectors to carry and deliver foreign DNA into specific host cells.

Micro-injection is a direct (vectorless) method of gene transfer in which recombinant DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell using a micro-pipette, without the involvement of any biological vector.

Answer: Micro-injection

questions.question: A researcher plots a temperature versus time graph for one complete cycle of a Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). The resulting curve displays three distinct temperature plateaus in sequence: Phase A at $94^{\circ}\text{C}$, Phase B at $54^{\circ}\text{C}$, and Phase C at $72^{\circ}\text{C}$. Which of the following primary molecular events occurs during Phase B?
options: Breaking of hydrogen bonds between the two strands of template DNA
Polymerization of deoxynucleotides by Taq polymerase
Hybridization of oligonucleotide primers to the single-stranded template DNA
Formation of phosphodiester bonds by DNA ligase to join DNA fragments
questions.solution:
The Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) consists of three main steps in each cycle, characterized by specific temperature requirements:

1. Denaturation (Phase A at $94^{\circ}\text{C}$): The double-stranded template DNA is heated to break the hydrogen bonds, resulting in single-stranded DNA.
2. Annealing (Phase B at $54^{\circ}\text{C}$): The temperature is lowered to allow two sets of oligonucleotide primers to hybridize (bind) to their complementary sequences on the single-stranded template DNA.
3. Extension (Phase C at $72^{\circ}\text{C}$): The temperature is raised to the optimum for Taq polymerase, which synthesizes the new DNA strand by adding deoxynucleotides.

Therefore, Phase B corresponds to the annealing step, where the hybridization of primers to the template DNA occurs. DNA ligase is not used in standard PCR.

Answer: Hybridization of oligonucleotide primers to the single-stranded template DNA

Without annealed primers, Taq polymerase cannot initiate the extension step, leading to a complete failure of amplification.

questions.question:
In a genetic engineering experiment, a bacterial culture is transformed with a plasmid vector containing an ampicillin resistance gene and a $\beta$-galactosidase gene (which has a cloning site). The culture is then plated on an agar medium containing ampicillin and a chromogenic substrate. After incubation, three distinct outcomes are observed for the bacterial cells:
(A) Cells that fail to grow and form colonies.
(B) Cells that grow and form blue-coloured colonies.
(C) Cells that grow and form white-coloured colonies.

Identify the biological nature of cells A, B, and C respectively.
options: A - Non-transformant; B - Recombinant transformant; C - Non-recombinant transformant
A - Non-transformant; B - Non-recombinant transformant; C - Recombinant transformant
A - Recombinant transformant; B - Non-transformant; C - Non-recombinant transformant
A - Non-recombinant transformant; B - Non-transformant; C - Recombinant transformant
questions.solution:
The agar medium contains ampicillin, an antibiotic. Cells that fail to grow (A) lack the plasmid entirely, meaning they do not possess the ampicillin resistance gene. These are non-transformants.

Cells that grow have successfully taken up the plasmid and are transformants. Among these, cells that form blue colonies (B) possess an intact $\beta$-galactosidase gene, which produces an enzyme that cleaves the chromogenic substrate to give a blue colour. This indicates no foreign DNA was inserted into the gene, making them non-recombinant transformants.

Cells that form white colonies (C) have an interrupted $\beta$-galactosidase gene due to the insertion of foreign DNA (insertional inactivation). They cannot produce the functional enzyme, so they remain colourless or white. These are recombinant transformants.

Answer: A - Non-transformant; B - Non-recombinant transformant; C - Recombinant transformant

questions.question: In 1963, two enzymes responsible for restricting the growth of bacteriophages in Escherichia coli were isolated. One of these enzymes cuts the viral DNA, while the host's own genomic DNA remains unaffected. What is the primary mechanism by which the bacterial host protects its own DNA from being cleaved by this restriction endonuclease?
options: The bacterial chromosome completely lacks the specific palindromic nucleotide sequences recognized by the enzyme.
A modifying enzyme adds methyl groups to specific bases within the recognition sites of the host DNA.
The restriction enzymes are sequestered within specialized membrane-bound organelles away from the nucleoid.
The host DNA is tightly enveloped by a continuous protective protein coat that prevents enzyme binding.
questions.solution:
In 1963, two enzymes responsible for restricting the growth of bacteriophages in Escherichia coli were isolated. This constitutes the restriction-modification system of bacteria.

One enzyme is a restriction endonuclease that cuts the viral DNA at specific recognition sites, effectively destroying the bacteriophage.

To protect its own genomic DNA from being cleaved by its own restriction enzymes, the bacteria produce a second enzyme (a methylase). This modifying enzyme adds methyl groups to specific bases within the same recognition sequences on the host DNA.

The methylation alters the structure of the recognition site, preventing the restriction endonuclease from binding and cutting the host DNA. Bacteria do not lack palindromic sequences, lack membrane-bound organelles to sequester enzymes, and do not have a continuous protective protein coat around their DNA.

Answer: A modifying enzyme adds methyl groups to specific bases within the recognition sites of the host DNA.

Answer: A modifying enzyme adds methyl groups to specific bases within the recognition sites of the host DNA.

questions.solution:
The isolation of pure DNA involves several sequential steps to remove other cellular components.

First, the cells must be broken open to release DNA along with other macromolecules. This is done by treating the sample with specific enzymes like lysozyme (for bacteria), cellulase (for plant cells), or chitinase (for fungus) (Step D).

Next, the RNA is removed by treatment with ribonuclease, and proteins are removed by treatment with protease (Step B).

Once the DNA is purified from these macromolecules, it is precipitated out by the addition of chilled ethanol (Step A).

Finally, the precipitated DNA, which appears as a collection of fine threads in the suspension, is removed by a process called spooling (Step C).

Thus, the correct chronological sequence is D, B, A, C.

Answer: D, B, A, C
questions.explanation:
The isolation of pure DNA involves several sequential steps to remove other cellular components.

First, the cells must be broken open to release DNA along with other macromolecules. This is done by treating the sample with specific enzymes like lysozyme (for bacteria), cellulase (for plant cells), or chitinase (for fungus) (Step D).

Next, the RNA is removed by treatment with ribonuclease, and proteins are removed by treatment with protease (Step B).

Once the DNA is purified from these macromolecules, it is precipitated out by the addition of chilled ethanol (Step A).

Finally, the precipitated DNA, which appears as a collection of fine threads in the suspension, is removed by a process called spooling (Step C).

Thus, the correct chronological sequence is D, B, A, C.

Answer: D, B, A, C

They will grow on ampicillin-containing medium but fail to grow on tetracycline-containing medium.

questions.solution:
In the pBR322 cloning vector, the restriction site for the enzyme Sal I is located within the tetracycline resistance ($tet^R$) gene.

When a foreign DNA fragment is ligated at the Sal I site, it causes insertional inactivation of the $tet^R$ gene. As a result, the recombinant plasmid loses its resistance to tetracycline.

However, the ampicillin resistance ($amp^R$) gene remains intact and functional. Therefore, the recombinant E. coli cells will be able to grow on an ampicillin-containing medium but will fail to grow on a tetracycline-containing medium.

The other options are incorrect because they either assume the $amp^R$ gene was inactivated, ignore the concept of insertional inactivation, or incorrectly assume both resistance genes are affected.

Answer: They will grow on ampicillin-containing medium but fail to grow on tetracycline-containing medium.

Which of the following steps of the PCR cycle will be the first to fail under these conditions?
options: Denaturation
Extension
Ligation
Annealing
questions.solution:
In a standard PCR cycle, the first step is denaturation, which requires a high temperature of $94^{\circ}\text{C}$ to separate the double-stranded DNA.

The second step is annealing, which requires the temperature to be lowered to $50-60^{\circ}\text{C}$ to allow the oligonucleotide primers to hybridize to the single-stranded DNA templates.

Because the temperature is continuously maintained at $94^{\circ}\text{C}$, the primers will not be able to bind to the template DNA. Therefore, annealing is the first step that will fail to occur. Extension cannot occur without successful annealing, and ligation is not a step in PCR.

Answer: Annealing

Sample B: $2\text{ cm}$

Assuming all other conditions are identical, which of the following represents the correct ascending order of the molecular weights of these DNA samples?
questions.question:
During an agarose gel electrophoresis experiment, three different double-stranded DNA samples, A, B, and C, were loaded into separate wells. After running the gel for a specific duration, the migration distances of the DNA bands from the wells were measured as follows:

Sample A: $4\text{ cm}$
Sample B: $2\text{ cm}$
Sample C: $6\text{ cm}$

Assuming all other conditions are identical, which of the following represents the correct ascending order of the molecular weights of these DNA samples?
options: C < A < B
B < A < C
A < B < C
A < C < B
questions.solution:
In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments separate according to their size through the sieving effect provided by the agarose gel.

The smaller the fragment size (lower molecular weight), the farther it moves from the well. Therefore, the migration distance of a DNA fragment is inversely proportional to its molecular weight.

Given the migration distances:
Sample C ($6\text{ cm}$) > Sample A ($4\text{ cm}$) > Sample B ($2\text{ cm}$)

The molecular weights will follow the reverse order:
Sample C < Sample A < Sample B.

Thus, the correct ascending order of their molecular weights is C < A < B.

Answer: C < A < B

A researcher programs a thermal cycler for a PCR reaction with the following temperature profile for 30 cycles:
Step 1: $94^{\circ}\text{C}$ for 1 minute
Step 2: $85^{\circ}\text{C}$ for 1 minute
Step 3: $72^{\circ}\text{C}$ for 2 minutes

The PCR fails to amplify the gene of interest. What is the most likely reason for this failure?
questions.question:
A researcher programs a thermal cycler for a PCR reaction with the following temperature profile for 30 cycles:
Step 1: $94^{\circ}\text{C}$ for 1 minute
Step 2: $85^{\circ}\text{C}$ for 1 minute
Step 3: $72^{\circ}\text{C}$ for 2 minutes

The PCR fails to amplify the gene of interest. What is the most likely reason for this failure?
options: The double-stranded DNA will fail to separate into single strands at $94^{\circ}\text{C}$.
The primers will fail to form stable hydrogen bonds with the template DNA at $85^{\circ}\text{C}$.
The Taq polymerase enzyme will denature and permanently lose its catalytic activity at $85^{\circ}\text{C}$.
The extension step will occur normally, but with a very high rate of mutation.
questions.solution:
The three steps of a PCR cycle are Denaturation, Annealing, and Extension.

Step 1 ($94^{\circ}\text{C}$) is the denaturation step, which successfully separates the double-stranded DNA.

Step 2 ($85^{\circ}\text{C}$) is intended to be the annealing step. However, the optimum temperature for primer annealing is typically between $40^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $60^{\circ}\text{C}$. At a high temperature of $85^{\circ}\text{C}$, the short oligonucleotide primers possess too much kinetic energy to form stable hydrogen bonds with the complementary regions of the template DNA.

Without annealed primers to provide a free $3'$-OH group, Taq polymerase cannot initiate synthesis during the extension step (Step 3 at $72^{\circ}\text{C}$), resulting in no amplification.

Taq polymerase is a thermostable enzyme isolated from Thermus aquaticus and remains active even at $94^{\circ}\text{C}$, so it will not denature at $85^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Answer: The primers will fail to form stable hydrogen bonds with the template DNA at $85^{\circ}\text{C}$.

questions.solution:
The restriction enzyme EcoRI recognizes the palindromic sequence GAATTC.

It cuts the DNA a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites, specifically between the bases Guanine (G) and Adenine (A) on both the opposite strands.

Restriction endonucleases function by cutting the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA, which means they break phosphodiester bonds, not hydrogen bonds.

Thus, EcoRI breaks phosphodiester bonds between G and A residues on both strands, leaving single-stranded overhanging stretches known as sticky ends.

questions.question: A forensic scientist recovers a minute amount of DNA from a crime scene and needs to obtain billions of identical copies of a specific DNA segment to proceed with the analysis. If this amplification must be performed entirely in vitro without using any living host cells or vectors, which of the following techniques should be employed?
options: Recombinant DNA technology
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
Gel electrophoresis
DNA fingerprinting
questions.solution:
The process of obtaining multiple identical copies of a specific DNA molecule in vitro (outside a living organism) without using host cells or vectors is achieved through the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). PCR allows for the exponential amplification of a target DNA segment using primers and a thermostable DNA polymerase.

Recombinant DNA technology (gene cloning) is an in vivo method that requires living host cells and vectors to multiply the DNA. Gel electrophoresis is a technique used to separate DNA fragments based on their size, not to amplify them. DNA fingerprinting is an analytical application that often relies on PCR for initial amplification, but PCR is the specific technique used to make the identical copies.

Answer: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the isolation of genetic material in recombinant DNA technology is incorrect?
options: Bacterial cells are treated with the enzyme lysozyme to degrade their cell walls and release DNA.
Fungal cells require treatment with chitinase to break open their cell walls for the release of intracellular macromolecules.
Animal cells must be treated with cellulase and pectinase to dissolve their complex cell walls prior to DNA isolation.
Plant cells are treated with cellulase to degrade their cellulosic cell walls to facilitate the release of genetic material.
questions.solution:
To isolate DNA, the cell must be broken open to release genetic material along with other macromolecules. This is achieved by treating the cells with specific enzymes that degrade their respective cell walls.

Bacterial cells are treated with lysozyme, plant cells with cellulase, and fungal cells with chitinase. However, animal cells lack a cell wall entirely; they are bounded only by a plasma membrane. Therefore, they do not require treatment with cell-wall degrading enzymes like cellulase or pectinase. The statement claiming animal cells need such enzymes to dissolve their cell walls is factually incorrect.

Answer: Animal cells must be treated with cellulase and pectinase to dissolve their complex cell walls prior to DNA isolation.

What will be the growth characteristics of the cells transformed with this recombinant plasmid when plated on different antibiotic-containing media?
questions.question: A piece of foreign DNA is ligated at the Sal I recognition site of the cloning vector pBR322. The resulting recombinant plasmid is then successfully introduced into E. coli cells. What will be the growth characteristics of the cells transformed with this recombinant plasmid when plated on different antibiotic-containing media?
options: They will grow on a medium containing tetracycline but fail to grow on a medium containing ampicillin.
They will grow on a medium containing ampicillin but fail to grow on a medium containing tetracycline.
They will grow on media containing both ampicillin and tetracycline.
They will fail to grow on media containing either ampicillin or tetracycline.
questions.solution:
In the cloning vector pBR322, the recognition site for the restriction enzyme Sal I is located within the tetracycline resistance gene.

When a piece of foreign DNA is ligated at the Sal I site, it causes insertional inactivation of the tetracycline resistance gene. The ampicillin resistance gene remains intact.

Therefore, the E. coli cells transformed with this recombinant plasmid will retain resistance to ampicillin but will lose resistance to tetracycline. As a result, they will grow on a medium containing ampicillin but will fail to grow on a medium containing tetracycline.

Answer: They will grow on a medium containing ampicillin but fail to grow on a medium containing tetracycline.

options: Spooling
Elution
Transformation
Downstream processing
questions.solution:
The separation of DNA fragments is carried out by gel electrophoresis. The separated DNA fragments can be visualized only after staining the DNA with ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation.

According to NCERT, the separated bands of DNA are cut out from the agarose gel and extracted from the gel piece. This specific step is known as elution.

Spooling is the extraction of precipitated DNA from a chilled ethanol suspension during the isolation of genetic material. Transformation is the introduction of recombinant DNA into a host cell. Answer: Elution

questions.question: A researcher is attempting to isolate pure DNA from a fungal cell for recombinant DNA technology. Which of the following represents the correct combination of treatments required to successfully extract and precipitate the purified DNA?
options: Cellulase, protease, ribonuclease, and chilled ethanol
Chitinase, protease, deoxyribonuclease, and chilled ethanol
Chitinase, protease, ribonuclease, and chilled ethanol
Lysozyme, ribonuclease, and chilled ethanol
questions.solution:
To isolate DNA from a fungal cell, the cell wall must first be broken down. Fungal cell walls are composed of chitin, so the enzyme chitinase is required (cellulase is for plant cells and lysozyme is for bacterial cells).

Once the cell is lysed, the extract contains macromolecules like RNA and proteins along with DNA. RNA is removed by treatment with ribonuclease, and proteins are removed by treatment with protease. Deoxyribonuclease (DNase) cannot be used as it would degrade the target DNA itself.

Finally, the purified DNA is precipitated by the addition of chilled ethanol.

Answer: Chitinase, protease, ribonuclease, and chilled ethanol

questions.solution:
Each cycle of Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) involves three main steps.

Extension is the final step, where a thermostable DNA polymerase adds deoxynucleotides to the primers, using the genomic DNA as a template to synthesise the new strand.

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(ii), (B)-(iii), and (C)-(i).

What will be the complete sequence of this recognition site on the complementary strand, read in the 3' $\rightarrow$ 5' direction?
options: 3' - T T C G A A - 5'
3' - A A G C T T - 5'
5' - T T C G A A - 3'
3' - U U C G A A - 5'
questions.solution:
A palindromic nucleotide sequence in DNA reads the same on the two strands when the orientation of reading is kept the same (e.g., 5' $\rightarrow$ 3').

If the first three bases on one strand are 5' - A A G, the complementary strand must also start with 5' - A A G when read in the 5' $\rightarrow$ 3' direction.

Thus, the complementary strand in the 5' $\rightarrow$ 3' direction is 5' - A A G C T T - 3'.

When this complementary strand is read in the 3' $\rightarrow$ 5' direction, the sequence is 3' - T T C G A A - 5'.

Answer: 3' - T T C G A A - 5'
questions.explanation:

Thus, the complementary strand in the 5' $\rightarrow$ 3' direction is 5' - A A G C T T - 3'.

When this complementary strand is read in the 3' $\rightarrow$ 5' direction, the sequence is 3' - T T C G A A - 5'.

Answer: 3' - T T C G A A - 5'

questions.question: A researcher prepares a standard Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) mixture but mistakenly adds normal human DNA polymerase instead of Taq polymerase isolated from Thermus aquaticus. The mixture is then subjected to a standard thermal cycle: $94^{\circ}\text{C}$ for 1 minute, $55^{\circ}\text{C}$ for 45 seconds, and $72^{\circ}\text{C}$ for 1 minute. Which specific step of the first PCR cycle will fail to produce its intended molecular outcome?
options: Extension
Denaturation
Annealing
Proofreading
questions.solution:
The first step of the PCR cycle is denaturation at $94^{\circ}\text{C}$, which relies solely on heat to break the hydrogen bonds between DNA strands. This step will occur successfully.

However, normal human DNA polymerase is not thermostable and will be irreversibly denatured (destroyed) by this high temperature.

The second step, annealing at $55^{\circ}\text{C}$, also occurs successfully because primers hybridize to the template DNA based on complementary base pairing, which does not require an enzyme.

The third step, extension at $72^{\circ}\text{C}$, requires an active DNA polymerase to synthesize the new strand. Since the human DNA polymerase was destroyed during the initial $94^{\circ}\text{C}$ step, the extension phase will fail to occur.

Answer: Extension

questions.solution:
In recombinant DNA technology, antibiotic resistance genes present on a plasmid act as selectable markers. They allow for the selection of transformants (cells that have taken up the plasmid) by permitting their growth on a selective medium containing the antibiotic, while non-transformants are eliminated.

Since the modified plasmid lacks antibiotic resistance genes, it cannot provide a selectable marker. Consequently, both transformed and non-transformed cells will grow equally well on a normal medium, making it impossible to distinguish or select the transformants.

The plasmid will still replicate because it has a functional 'ori'. Ligation of foreign DNA is still possible due to the presence of cloning sites. The host cell will not die upon transformation unless exposed to an antibiotic it is not resistant to.

Answer: It will be impossible to select the transformants from the non-transformants.

questions.q: Which of the following double-stranded DNA sequences represents a typical palindromic recognition site for a restriction endonuclease?
questions.question: Which of the following double-stranded DNA sequences represents a typical palindromic recognition site for a restriction endonuclease?
options:
$5' - \text{GATTAG} - 3'$
$3' - \text{CTAATC} - 5'$

$5' - \text{GAATTC} - 3'$
$3' - \text{GAATTC} - 5'$

$5' - \text{GGATCC} - 3'$
$3' - \text{CCTAGG} - 5'$

$5' - \text{GTCGTC} - 3'$
$3' - \text{CAGCAG} - 5'$
questions.solution:
A DNA palindrome is a sequence of base pairs that reads the same on the two strands when the orientation of reading is kept the same. For example, if we read $5' \to 3'$ on the top strand, the bottom strand must also read the exact same sequence in the $5' \to 3'$ direction.

In the sequence $5' - \text{GGATCC} - 3'$ and $3' - \text{CCTAGG} - 5'$, reading the top strand from $5' \to 3'$ gives GGATCC. Reading the bottom strand from $5' \to 3'$ also gives GGATCC. Furthermore, the two strands correctly follow the rules of complementary base pairing (G pairs with C, A pairs with T).

The sequence $5' - \text{GATTAG} - 3'$ is a word palindrome on a single strand but does not read the same on its complementary strand. The sequence with $3' - \text{GAATTC} - 5'$ on the bottom strand lacks complementary base pairing entirely.

Answer: $5' - \text{GGATCC} - 3'$
$3' - \text{CCTAGG} - 5'$

Determine the total number of visible bands on the gel and identify the size of the fragment that will be found closest to the anode.
questions.question:
A linear DNA molecule of $5\text{ kb}$ is fully digested with a restriction endonuclease that has two recognition sites located at $1\text{ kb}$ and $3\text{ kb}$ from one end. The digested DNA is then subjected to agarose gel electrophoresis.

Determine the total number of visible bands on the gel and identify the size of the fragment that will be found closest to the anode.
options: $3$ bands, with the $1\text{ kb}$ fragment closest to the anode
$3$ bands, with the $2\text{ kb}$ fragment closest to the anode
$2$ bands, with the $1\text{ kb}$ fragment closest to the anode
$2$ bands, with the $2\text{ kb}$ fragment closest to the anode
questions.solution:
A linear DNA molecule of $5\text{ kb}$ with restriction sites at $1\text{ kb}$ and $3\text{ kb}$ from one end will be cleaved into three fragments. The sizes of these fragments are $1\text{ kb}$ (from $0$ to $1\text{ kb}$), $2\text{ kb}$ (from $1\text{ kb}$ to $3\text{ kb}$), and $2\text{ kb}$ (from $3\text{ kb}$ to $5\text{ kb}$).

During agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments separate based on their size. The two $2\text{ kb}$ fragments have the same size and will co-migrate, appearing as a single band on the gel. The $1\text{ kb}$ fragment will form a second band. Therefore, a total of $2$ visible bands will be observed.

Smaller DNA fragments experience less resistance from the agarose gel matrix and travel farther from the loading wells. Thus, the smallest fragment ($1\text{ kb}$) will move the fastest and be found closest to the anode (the positive electrode).

Answer: $2$ bands, with the $1\text{ kb}$ fragment closest to the anode

questions.q: A researcher isolates a linear double-stranded DNA fragment that possesses short, single-stranded overhanging stretches at both of its ends. Which of the following statements correctly describes the enzyme responsible for generating this specific type of DNA fragment?
questions.question: A researcher isolates a linear double-stranded DNA fragment that possesses short, single-stranded overhanging stretches at both of its ends. Which of the following statements correctly describes the enzyme responsible for generating this specific type of DNA fragment?
options: It is an exonuclease that removed nucleotides from the terminal ends of the DNA.
It is a restriction endonuclease that cut the DNA strands a little away from the centre of the palindromic site.
It is a restriction endonuclease that cut both DNA strands exactly at the centre of the palindromic site.
It is a DNA ligase that failed to fully join the complementary strands.
questions.solution:
The single-stranded overhanging stretches at the ends of the DNA fragment are known as 'sticky ends'.

Sticky ends are produced by restriction endonucleases when they cut the DNA strands a little away from the centre of the palindromic recognition site, but between the same two bases on opposite strands.

Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends but do not specifically generate these palindromic sticky ends. Endonucleases that cut exactly at the centre of the palindromic site produce blunt ends, not sticky ends. DNA ligase joins DNA fragments together; it does not cut them.

Answer: It is a restriction endonuclease that cut the DNA strands a little away from the centre of the palindromic site.

options: They will be resistant to both ampicillin and tetracycline.
They will be sensitive to both ampicillin and tetracycline.

questions.solution:
In the cloning vector pBR322, the recognition site for the restriction endonuclease BamHI is located within the tetracycline resistance gene ($tet^{R}$).

However, the ampicillin resistance gene ($amp^{R}$) remains intact. Therefore, the recombinant transformants will be resistant to ampicillin but sensitive to tetracycline.

Options suggesting resistance to both assume no insertional inactivation, while those suggesting sensitivity to ampicillin confuse the location of the BamHI site with sites like PvuI or PstI.

Answer: They will be resistant to ampicillin but sensitive to tetracycline.

This plasmid is then transformed into competent, ampicillin-sensitive E. coli cells. If these cells are subsequently plated on an agar medium containing ampicillin, what will be the most likely observed result after standard incubation?
questions.question: A researcher constructs a recombinant plasmid containing an intact ampicillin resistance gene ($amp^{R}$) but accidentally introduces a mutation that completely inactivates its origin of replication ('ori'). This plasmid is then transformed into competent, ampicillin-sensitive E. coli cells. If these cells are subsequently plated on an agar medium containing ampicillin, what will be the most likely observed result after standard incubation?
options: Normal colonies will appear because the ampicillin resistance gene is intact.
Colonies will appear but they will lack the gene of interest.
The bacteria will undergo lysis immediately upon transformation.
No colonies will appear on the plate because the plasmid cannot multiply and be maintained in the progeny cells.
questions.solution:
The origin of replication ('ori') is a specific DNA sequence responsible for initiating replication. Any piece of DNA linked to this sequence can be made to replicate within the host cells.

If the 'ori' is inactivated, the plasmid cannot replicate independently. Even though the plasmid carries an intact ampicillin resistance gene, it will not be duplicated when the host cell divides. Consequently, the plasmid will be diluted and lost in the progeny cells, leaving them sensitive to ampicillin.

Therefore, the cells will fail to multiply and form colonies on the ampicillin-containing medium. Option 1 is incorrect because an intact resistance gene is useless if it cannot be maintained in the dividing population. Option 2 is incorrect because no colonies will form at all. Option 3 is incorrect because transformation itself does not cause immediate lysis.

Answer: No colonies will appear on the plate because the plasmid cannot multiply and be maintained in the progeny cells.

questions.question:
Consider the two double-stranded DNA fragments produced after the digestion of a linear DNA molecule by a specific enzyme:

Fragment I:
$5^{\prime}-\dots \text{G}-3^{\prime}$
$3^{\prime}-\dots \text{CTTAA}-5^{\prime}$

Fragment II:
$5^{\prime}-\text{AATTC}\dots -3^{\prime}$

options: The enzyme involved is an exonuclease that removes nucleotides from the free ends to create these fragments.
The enzyme is an endonuclease that recognises the palindromic sequence $5^{\prime}-\text{GAATTC}-3^{\prime}$ and cuts away from the centre of the symmetry.
The original intact sequence was $5^{\prime}-\text{GATATC}-3^{\prime}$ and the enzyme produced blunt ends.
The enzyme cuts the DNA exactly at the centre of the palindromic sequence to generate these overhanging stretches.
questions.solution:
By aligning the complementary overhanging stretches (sticky ends) of Fragment I and Fragment II, the original intact DNA sequence can be reconstructed as $5^{\prime}-\text{GAATTC}-3^{\prime}$ on one strand and $3^{\prime}-\text{CTTAAG}-5^{\prime}$ on the complementary strand.

EcoRI cuts the DNA between the bases G and A on both the strands. This cut is made slightly away from the centre of the palindromic sequence, which results in the formation of single-stranded overhanging stretches called sticky ends. Therefore, the enzyme does not cut at the centre and does not produce blunt ends.

Answer: The enzyme is an endonuclease that recognises the palindromic sequence $5^{\prime}-\text{GAATTC}-3^{\prime}$ and cuts away from the centre of the symmetry.

By aligning the complementary overhanging stretches (sticky ends) of Fragment I and Fragment II, the original intact DNA sequence can be reconstructed as $5^{\prime}-\text{GAATTC}-3^{\prime}$ on one strand and $3^{\prime}-\text{CTTAAG}-5^{\prime}$ on the complementary strand.

In the pBR322 cloning vector, the restriction site for $Pst\text{ I}$ is located within the $amp^R$ (ampicillin resistance) gene.

When a foreign DNA fragment is inserted at the $Pst\text{ I}$ site, it causes insertional inactivation of the $amp^R$ gene. As a result, the recombinant plasmid loses ampicillin resistance but retains tetracycline resistance (since the $tet^R$ gene remains intact).

Therefore, the transformants containing the recombinant plasmid will be able to grow on a tetracycline-containing medium but will fail to grow on an ampicillin-containing medium.

Which enzyme should the researcher choose for the cloning experiment, and what will be the immediate consequence of successful insertion?
questions.question: A researcher wants to clone a foreign gene into a plasmid vector. The vector has three recognition sites for restriction enzyme X and a single recognition site for restriction enzyme Y. The recognition site for enzyme Y is located within the tetracycline resistance gene ($tet^{R}$). Which enzyme should the researcher choose for the cloning experiment, and what will be the immediate consequence of successful insertion?
options: Enzyme X, because multiple recognition sites increase the probability of successful ligation.
Enzyme Y, resulting in the insertional inactivation of the tetracycline resistance gene.
Enzyme X, resulting in the insertional inactivation of the origin of replication.
Enzyme Y, resulting in the generation of several vector fragments.
questions.solution:
In order to link the alien DNA, a cloning vector needs to have very few, preferably single, recognition sites for the commonly used restriction enzymes.

Presence of more than one recognition site within the vector (as with enzyme X) will generate several fragments, which will complicate the gene cloning process. Therefore, the researcher must avoid enzyme X and choose enzyme Y, which has a single recognition site.

Since the recognition site for enzyme Y is located within the tetracycline resistance gene, the insertion of the foreign DNA at this site will disrupt the gene. This phenomenon is known as insertional inactivation, and it leads to the loss of tetracycline resistance in the recombinant plasmid.

Answer: Enzyme Y, resulting in the insertional inactivation of the tetracycline resistance gene.

questions.question: A biotechnologist wants to use Agrobacterium tumefaciens to deliver a desirable gene into a dicot plant. To ensure that the plant does not develop crown gall disease after the gene transfer, which specific modification must be made to the wild-type Ti plasmid?
options: The disease-causing genes must be removed to disarm the plasmid while keeping the transfer mechanism intact
The entire T-DNA region must be deleted to prevent the integration of any bacterial DNA into the plant genome
The origin of replication (ori) must be excised to stop the plasmid from multiplying inside the plant cells
Antibiotic resistance genes must be added to actively suppress the tumor-inducing property of the bacteria
questions.solution:
The correct modification is to disarm the Ti plasmid by removing its disease-causing (tumor-inducing) genes.

In nature, the T-DNA of the Ti plasmid carries genes that transform normal plant cells into tumor cells. To use it as a safe cloning vector, these pathogenic genes are removed while the sequences required for DNA transfer are kept intact. The gene of interest is then inserted into this disarmed T-DNA.

Deleting the entire T-DNA would prevent any gene transfer. Excising the origin of replication would stop the plasmid from replicating in the bacterial host. Adding antibiotic resistance genes helps in selection but does not prevent tumor formation.

Answer: The disease-causing genes must be removed to disarm the plasmid while keeping the transfer mechanism intact

What will be the most likely consequence on the gene amplification process?
questions.question: A researcher sets up a standard Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) to amplify a gene of interest. However, instead of adding Taq polymerase, they mistakenly add ordinary DNA polymerase isolated from Escherichia coli. All other components (template DNA, primers, and dNTPs) are correctly added. What will be the most likely consequence on the gene amplification process?
options: Amplification will occur but at a much slower rate.
The primers will fail to anneal to the template DNA.
No amplification will occur as the enzyme will be denatured during the first cycle.
Continuous amplification will occur but with a high rate of mutations.
questions.solution:
PCR involves three main steps: Denaturation, Annealing, and Extension. The denaturation step requires a high temperature (around $94^{\circ}\text{C}$) to separate the double-stranded template DNA.

Ordinary DNA polymerase from E. coli is not thermostable. It will be denatured and permanently destroyed during the very first high-temperature denaturation step. Consequently, no extension of primers can occur, resulting in no amplification of the gene.

This is why Taq polymerase, isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus, is required for PCR, as it remains active during the repeated high-temperature cycles.

Answer: No amplification will occur as the enzyme will be denatured during the first cycle.

Answer: No amplification will occur as the enzyme will be denatured during the first cycle.

questions.q: A PCR machine is programmed to perform repeated thermal cycles with temperatures set sequentially at $94^{\circ}\text{C}$, $54^{\circ}\text{C}$, and $72^{\circ}\text{C}$. Which of the following primary biochemical events occurs when the reaction mixture is held at $94^{\circ}\text{C}$?
questions.question: A PCR machine is programmed to perform repeated thermal cycles with temperatures set sequentially at $94^{\circ}\text{C}$, $54^{\circ}\text{C}$, and $72^{\circ}\text{C}$. Which of the following primary biochemical events occurs when the reaction mixture is held at $94^{\circ}\text{C}$?
options: Binding of oligonucleotide primers to the template
Separation of the double-stranded DNA into single strands
Polymerization of deoxynucleotides to synthesize a new strand
Joining of discontinuous DNA fragments by ligase
questions.solution:
A standard Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) cycle consists of three steps: denaturation, annealing, and extension.

The highest temperature in the cycle, typically around $94^{\circ}\text{C}$, is used for the denaturation step. At this temperature, the hydrogen bonds between the base pairs of the double-stranded template DNA break, resulting in the separation of the two strands.

The temperature is then lowered to around $54^{\circ}\text{C}$ for the annealing of oligonucleotide primers, and subsequently raised to $72^{\circ}\text{C}$ for the extension step, where Taq polymerase synthesizes the new DNA strand. DNA ligase is not used in PCR.

Answer: Separation of the double-stranded DNA into single strands

The fragments in Band I are positively charged, whereas those in Band III are negatively charged.
questions.solution:
During agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments separate according to their size due to the sieving effect of the agarose gel. The smaller the fragment size, the farther it moves from the well.

All DNA fragments are negatively charged and move towards the anode; separation is based purely on size, not differences in charge.

Therefore, the correct inference is that Band III contains the smallest DNA fragments.

Answer: Band III contains the smallest DNA fragments among the three bands.

questions.question: In a recombinant DNA experiment, a plasmid vector and a segment of foreign DNA are both digested with the restriction enzyme EcoRI to generate complementary sticky ends. When these fragments are mixed, they transiently pair up. Which enzyme must be added to permanently join these DNA fragments, and what specific chemical bond does it catalyze to seal the backbone?
options: DNA ligase and Phosphodiester bond
DNA polymerase and Phosphodiester bond
DNA ligase and Hydrogen bond
Restriction endonuclease and Phosphodiester bond
questions.solution:
When DNA fragments are cut with the same restriction enzyme, they produce complementary sticky ends that can form hydrogen bonds between base pairs on their own. However, this pairing is temporary and easily broken.

To permanently join the fragments and form a stable recombinant DNA molecule, the enzyme DNA ligase is required. DNA ligase seals the sugar-phosphate backbone by catalyzing the formation of a covalent phosphodiester bond between the 3'-hydroxyl and 5'-phosphate ends of adjacent nucleotides.

DNA polymerase synthesizes new DNA strands rather than joining pre-existing fragments, and restriction endonucleases cut DNA rather than joining it.

Answer: DNA ligase and Phosphodiester bond

questions.solution:
In the final step of DNA isolation, purified DNA precipitates out after the addition of chilled ethanol. This precipitation can be seen as a collection of fine threads in the suspension.

The physical process of removing these precipitated DNA threads from the suspension, typically using a glass rod, is known as spooling.

Elution refers to the extraction of separated DNA fragments from an agarose gel piece, which is a different process. Room temperature ethanol or chilled chloroform will not effectively precipitate the DNA in this context.

Answer: Chilled ethanol and Spooling

The cells are first plated on a medium containing ampicillin, and then the growing colonies are replica-plated onto a medium containing tetracycline. What will be the growth pattern of the recombinant colonies on these two antibiotic plates?
questions.question: A researcher ligates a foreign DNA fragment into the $Sal\text{I}$ restriction site of the standard pBR322 vector. The resulting plasmid mixture is transformed into host E. coli cells. The cells are first plated on a medium containing ampicillin, and then the growing colonies are replica-plated onto a medium containing tetracycline. What will be the growth pattern of the recombinant colonies on these two antibiotic plates?
options: They will grow on the ampicillin plate but not on the tetracycline plate.
They will grow on both the ampicillin and tetracycline plates.
They will grow on the tetracycline plate but not on the ampicillin plate.
They will not grow on either of the antibiotic plates.
questions.solution:
In the pBR322 vector, the $Sal\text{I}$ restriction site is located within the tetracycline resistance gene.

Insertion of a foreign DNA fragment at this site causes insertional inactivation of the tetracycline resistance gene, making the recombinant plasmids sensitive to tetracycline. The ampicillin resistance gene remains intact.

Therefore, the recombinant E. coli colonies will be resistant to ampicillin but sensitive to tetracycline. They will grow on the ampicillin-containing medium but will fail to grow when replica-plated onto the tetracycline-containing medium.

Non-recombinants would grow on both plates, while non-transformants would not grow on either.

Answer: They will grow on the ampicillin plate but not on the tetracycline plate.

questions.question:

To generate such ends, what must be true about the specific location where this enzyme cuts the DNA double helix?
options: It cuts exactly at the centre of the palindromic site on both strands.
It cuts between different bases on the opposite strands of the DNA.
It cuts a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites, between the same two bases on opposite strands.
It cuts only one strand of the double helix, leaving the other strand intact.
questions.solution:
Restriction enzymes can produce either blunt ends or sticky ends depending on where they cut the DNA.

To produce sticky ends (single-stranded overhanging stretches), the enzyme must cut the DNA a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites, but strictly between the same two bases on the opposite strands. This staggered cut leaves single-stranded portions at the ends.

Cutting exactly at the centre of the palindromic site (Option 1) produces blunt ends. Restriction endonucleases typically cut between the same two bases on opposite strands, making Option 2 incorrect. Cutting only one strand (Option 4) does not cleave the DNA into fragments and is not characteristic of restriction endonuclease digestion.

Answer: It cuts a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites, between the same two bases on opposite strands.
